correctness.rationale: For the standard cross-polytope, every facet has support number \(1/\sqrt n\), \((n-1)\)-volume \(\sqrt n/(n-1)!\), and mass \(1/(n-1)!\). Adjacent facets differ in one sign, their ridge has \((n-2)\)-volume \(\sqrt{n-1}/(n-2)!\), and their normal-angle sine is \(2\sqrt{n-1}/n\), giving conductance \(1/[2(n-2)!]\). Thus \(c/m=(n-1)/2\) and the facet network is the Boolean \(n\)-cube. Walsh characters of degree \(k\) have ordinary cube-Laplacian eigenvalue \(2k\), hence generalized eigenvalue \((n-1)k\). Antipodal evenness is exactly even Walsh degree. These calculations cover \(n=2\) as well as \(n\ge3\), prove completeness through the Walsh basis, and establish the stated multiplicities. No unverified variational theorem or finite experiment is needed for the infinite family; the checker only stress-tests the closed formulas.

value.rationale: The regular cross-polytope is a canonical origin-symmetric, highly nonsimple test object for the newly introduced facet-network spectrum. The result gives the complete spectrum and multiplicities in all dimensions, not a single sample value, by exposing an exact Boolean-hypercube model. It also shows a qualitative contrast with the flat parallelotope spectrum and, for \(n\ge3\), a polarity asymmetry between the cube and its polar cross-polytope. This supplies a reusable benchmark for computations and for testing conjectures about the new centro-affine spectral invariant.
